blocks.text: I add an eighth, that of Knatchbull, who in his Animadverss. in Nov. Testam. on this passage, p. 6 ff., thinks that the ἀκρίδας [akridas] were κεράτια [keratia], siliquas [carob pods], the fruit of the Ceratonia tree, or Pseudo-Acacia, which the Germans call Iohannis-Brodt, i.e. John's bread. He was moved chiefly by this reason: that the tree is common in the desert in which John is said to have lived, and which today is called the desert of St John. To state this opinion will be the same as to refute it, for no argument can prove that ἀκρίδας [akridas] and κεράτια [keratia] mean the same thing.

That locusts are still today dried and preserved with salt in the East is also reported by Rauwolf and Niebuhr (p. 171); their testimonies and those of others are collected by Oedmann, fasc. 2, Chapter 6, p. 106. 107. Russell, Natural History of Aleppo, p. 62: It may not be omiss to mention, that the Arabs eat this locust when fresh, and also salt them up as a delicacy.

Forsskål in Descript. Animall. p. 81: "The Bedouin of Egypt roast grylli of this species [جراد [jarād]] alive over coals, and then, throwing away the wings and legs, eat them greedily. In Arabia Felix, between Mocha and Taizz, I saw women and boys intent on hunting these little birds; they strung them, up to 100, on a thread drawn through the thorax, and offered them for the price of ½ Chomas. The whole bundle is roasted. Not only the legs and wings of the gryllus are torn off, but also the intestines, which are laid bare when the head is pulled out a little. Certainly a juiceless food, yet harmless; except that its excessive use causes sluggish blood, or a melancholic temperament, as the Arabs maintain, which they call Souda. For the rest, I heard a ridiculous defence of this food: the gryllus feeds on pure, useful plants, indeed even ones of medicinal power; it therefore cannot be otherwise than that it becomes wholly wholesome itself. Yet the inhabitants consume too little of them to diminish the number of this harmful swarm even slightly." For more on the eating of locusts see Niebuhr, p. 171, Hasselquist, p. 452 ff., Höst, p. 301, and Oedmann, fasc. 2, Chapter 6, p. 105 ff. and fasc. 6, Chapter 8, p. 78.
